The findings of this review suggest that although surgical fixation is a reliable method for achieving radiographic union, its impact on clinical function appears modest. Surgeons should counsel patients that operative management carries a substantial risk of complications without a superior functional result compared to nonoperative immobilization, particularly in chronic or delayed settings. Only the Bauer et al study, which uniquely enrolled only those acromial fractures managed acutely (within 6 weeks of injury) and excluded any patients who had first undergone a trial of nonoperative care in the surgical cohort, demonstrated statistically significant improvements in function and ROM compared to the nonoperative group. Generally, the operative management cohort in all other studies were composed of patients that initially failed nonoperative management, and no significant differences in functional outcomes were reported in those studies. This may serve as a confounding variable and further indicates the need for further study of acute operative management. The allocation of failed nonoperative patients to the surgical arm may result in artificially favorable outcomes in the nonoperative group. Considering only the outcomes of patients that underwent surgical repair after failed nonoperative treatment in the surgical cohort could harm the internal validity of direct comparisons between nonoperative and operative treatment pathways. Acute ORIF should continue to be explored in future studies, as it allows a stronger comparison between the 2 treatment modalities to better elucidate the relationship between the functional outcomes of surgical and nonoperative management. In addition, heterogeneity in fracture classification may further impact the ability to derive impactful conclusions on ASF management after rTSA. Given that the Levy classification system has greater interobserver reliability than the Crosby classification, we propose that the Levy system is used in future studies to promote greater homogeneity in the study of ASFs and allow for robust review and possible meta-analysis. Future studies that report CM, ASES, SST, pain, and Single Assessment Numeric Evaluation outcome measures with larger sample sizes and fractures classified in accordance with the Levy system would allow for a direct comparison of surgical and conservative management. This would allow surgeons to better distinguish between treatment plans for their ASF patients. In the current study, dual plate fixation was significantly more used than a single plate technique. A 2022 review of ASF fixation constructs by Cassidy et al reported that dual plate fixation was more commonly used for Levy type III fractures than for more lateral Levy type I and II fractures. Overall, they investigated 17 fractures, finding dual plate techniques for 8 fractures, and single plating for 9 fractures, noting union in 14 out of 15 studied fractures. With a lack of direct comparison of functional outcomes between fixation techniques in the studies included in both reviews, it is difficult to determine if an optimal fixation technique exists. Biomechanical studies have demonstrated that the dual plate technique is a stronger fixation construct, but there currently is a paucity of functional clinical outcomes stratified by fixation technique. Further studies should investigate functional outcomes between single and dual plate fixation. A major limitation of this review is the small sample sizes and the retrospective nature of these studies. Larger sample sizes with unified outcome measures would be necessary to perform a meta-analysis of surgical management compared to operative management. Currently, meta-analysis is attainable for nonoperative management compared to nonfracture groups, as demonstrated by Cui et al Conclusion In the studies included in this review, Levy type III fractures were treated surgically at a higher rate than other fracture types due to poor function and pain. Surgical management of ASFs was largely reserved for patients who failed nonoperative treatment. Improvement of functional outcomes in surgical intervention compared to nonoperative treatment was found only in acute surgical intervention. No statistically significant difference was found when comparing delayed surgical intervention and nonoperative treatment. Surgical management was associated with significantly higher union rates than nonoperative management. However, functional improvements were largely modest and comparable to nonoperative management in delayed cases, and the benefits of surgery must be weighed against a high complication rate. Double plate fixation was the predominant surgical technique for ASF after rTSA. The use of the Levy classification system and assessment of uniform functional outcomes in future studies would allow for stronger analysis of the comparative impacts of surgical and nonoperative treatment of ASF after rTSA.
